name: ABBV-295

lead: ABBV-295 (also GUB014295) is an amylin analogue injected under the skin, developed by AbbVie for obesity. People follow it for fullness-driven fat loss.

Amylin analogues mimic the hormone amylin, which promotes satiety and slows gastric emptying, so the chain is more fullness, lower intake, then weight loss and a leaner body. Registered trials include several phase 1 studies and a phase 2 trial of 360 adults that began recruiting in August 2026; no results are public.

paras: It is given by subcutaneous injection and is available only in clinical trials.
Safety data are not published. The drug is not approved.

angle.text: ABBV-295 is AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue, followed by fat-loss readers as a fullness-based route to a leaner body. It mimics a satiety hormone to cut intake. It is in early trials with no results out.

lead: ABBV-295 (also GUB014295) is an investigational amylin analogue given by subcutaneous injection, being developed by AbbVie for obesity. It is not approved [1][2]. Drugs in this class aim to reduce appetite and body weight, and weight loss is the route by which they bear on appearance: a lower body fat percentage shows in a leaner face, a more defined jawline and a visible physique.

Registered trials include Phase 1 studies in adults with obesity, in Japanese participants with overweight or obesity, and in women taking oral contraceptives, and a Phase 2 trial in 360 adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities that began recruiting in August 2026 [3][2][4][5]. A 2026 narrative review of amylin-based therapies names ABBV-295 among long-acting amylin-based agents that it describes as having demonstrated clinically meaningful weight loss with generally favorable tolerability; trial-level results specific to ABBV-295 were not located in a published paper [1]. A registered psoriasis study lists targeted therapies and is not described as an ABBV-295 efficacy trial [6].

paras: Amylin is co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells. It slows gastric emptying, suppresses glucagon secretion and promotes meal termination through central mechanisms [1]. Amylin analogues mimic this hormone to produce earlier fullness and lower food intake.

Pramlintide, the first approved amylin analogue, established proof of concept but was limited by modest efficacy and frequent dosing; newer long-acting analogues, including cagrilintide, eloralintide, petrelintide, MET-233i, ABBV-295 and AZD6234, are in development, along with combinations such as cagrilintide with semaglutide [1].

AbbVie's program is registered under the codes ABBV-295 and GUB014295. The first Phase 1 study in adults with obesity began in November 2025 [2]. Additional Phase 1 studies registered in early 2026 examine tolerability and pharmacokinetics in Japanese participants and the effect of the drug on oral contraceptive pharmacokinetics in women [3][5]. A Phase 2 safety and efficacy trial in adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities began in August 2026 [4]. The 2026 review places the compound within the wave of amylin-based agents seen as a possible addition to incretin therapies such as semaglutide for obesity, whose management the review says incretin therapies have transformed [1].

Phase 1 trial NCT07291232 (about 80 adults with obesity) assesses adverse events and pharmacokinetics and began in November 2025 [2]. NCT07514260 studies about 24 Japanese participants with overweight or obesity and NCT07414784, a completed study of about 20 women, examines interaction with oral contraceptives [3][5]. Phase 2 trial NCT07752979 is recruiting about 360 adults [4]. Peer-reviewed results from these trials were not located.
A 2026 review of amylin analogues for obesity provides class background and lists ABBV-295 among agents reported to have shown clinically meaningful weight loss [1].

Safety data specific to ABBV-295 have not been published in the sources located. Registered Phase 1 trials list adverse events and pharmacokinetics as their outcomes [2]. The drug is unapproved and available only in clinical studies; the review describes amylin-based therapies in general as having favorable tolerability [1].

timeline.event: Phase 1 trial in adults with obesity begins (November).[2]
Japanese Phase 1 and oral-contraceptive interaction studies begin; Phase 2 obesity trial starts recruiting in August.[3][4][5]
